result.summary: Pausanias describes the temples and monuments on and around Larissa, the citadel of Argos, including a three-eyed wooden Zeus. He then follows the road toward Tegea past Mount Lycone, Mount Chaon, the source of the Erasinus, Cenchreæ and Hysiæ.

scenes.title: The citadel Larissa at Argos
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the temples, race-course and tombs on the way up Larissa, and explains the three-eyed Zeus.

scenes.title: The road to Tegea
scenes.summary: Along the road to Tegea he notes Lycone, Chaon, the Erasinus spring, Cenchreæ and the battle tomb at Hysiæ.

alias_notes.explanation: Cult title from the place called Ridge.

notable_quotes.reason: Homeric line used to show Zeus rules the underworld, explaining the three eyes.

analysis.text: The passage shows Pausanias's habit of pairing monuments with local legend and explaining odd cult images rationally.
He dates the battle at Hysiæ by Athenian rulers and Olympiads, showing how Greeks fixed events chronologically.

fun_facts.text: Larissa, the Argos citadel, is still crowned by a medieval fortress built on ancient foundations.

language_notes.text: "Ridge" and "Ridgeway" translate a Greek place-name; the epithet Apollo of the Ridgeway comes from the spot where the temple stands.
"Debarred from marriage" means the prophetess must stay unmarried, kept chaste for the god's service.
Alludes to the Iliad, where Athene clears the mist from Diomede's eyes so he can recognise gods on the battlefield.
Refers to the Danaids, who killed their cousins, the sons of Ægyptus, on their wedding night at their father Danaus's command.
"Tutelary" means serving as guardian or protector.
Proserpine is the Roman name for Persephone, queen of the dead; the translator uses it where Greek text would say Persephone.
Orthian Artemis was a cult title of the goddess, probably meaning 'upright'; the epithet is attached to her worship at several places.
The text says the Erasinus rises here, then compares it to the Rheti, which flow underground and re-emerge. Pausanias is referring to a belief that the river flows underground from Stymphalus.
'Medley' translates the festival's Greek name, Tyrbe, meaning confusion or disorder; the name suggests a mixed or tumultuous celebration.
Dating by Olympiad: Greeks counted years in four-year cycles from the first Olympic games. 'The course' means the foot race.
'The reverse happened' means the Lacedæmonians were defeated here, contrasting with their earlier victory claimed elsewhere.

context_notes.text: Larissa was the citadel of Argos; the name is Pelasgian-sounding and also borne by several Thessalian towns.
The Nemean games honoured Zeus and were one of the great Panhellenic festivals; Argos held its own games for Hera.
Sthenelus was Diomede's companion at Troy and an Argive leader, so bringing the statue to Argos is natural.
Æschylus was the Athenian tragic playwright, born at Eleusis.
Tegea lay in eastern Arcadia and was an important route between Argos and Sparta territory.
Polycletus was a famous Argive sculptor of the fifth century BC, best known for bronze statues.
Hysiæ was fought between Argos and Sparta; Pausanias treats it as an Argive victory, commemorated by a shared tomb.
Pisistratus was the tyrant of Athens in the sixth century BC, which helps place the battle in time.

literary_notes.text: The odd third eye in the forehead is a striking visual detail that prompts the explanation which follows.
Pausanias speaks as a cautious traveller-scholar, offering a reasoned guess ("one might conjecture") instead of asserting a fact.
The three eyes symbolise Zeus's rule over heaven, the underworld and the sea.
Pausanias adopts a guidebook tone, addressing the traveller directly and organising the account by directions along a road.
The author's candour about local ignorance shows his careful, sceptical habit of reporting only what informants can support.
